rankTracking.title: SEO Rank Tracker for Monitoring Keyword Rankings
rankTracking.subtitle: Your real Google positions recorded automatically every day — SEO rank monitoring across keyword, location, and device, with ranking history and alerts when positions move
rankTracking.whatItDoes: Rank tracking is the practice of recording where a domain appears in Google results for a chosen set of keywords, then watching how those positions change over time. SeeO runs this on a fixed daily schedule: it checks each tracked keyword against live Google results, stores the outcome, and compares it with the previous record. The value sits in the time dimension. A one-off rank check tells you where you stand today; a recorded history tells you whether the work you shipped last month actually moved anything. Every keyword keeps its own dated series, so the question "are we improving?" becomes a chart instead of an argument. This SEO rank tracker measures four dimensions at once — keyword, domain, location, and device. Desktop and mobile are stored as separate series, and each location is its own series, which is what makes local and international position tracking meaningful: the same keyword can hold a top-three position on desktop in one city while sitting on page three on mobile in another. Positions are read to a depth of 100 results. Movements that cross the alert threshold generate an in-app alert, so a drop off page one or a jump into the top three surfaces without you opening a report.

tracks.intro: Every rank record is identified by four independent dimensions. Change any one of them and you are looking at a different series — which is exactly the point, because Google does not return the same results for the same words everywhere.

items.name: Keyword
items.body: Each tracked keyword is an independent series. You decide which terms matter: revenue pages, campaign terms, or the head terms your competitors are fighting over.

items.name: Domain
items.body: Every check is measured against one target domain. Your tracked keyword list also feeds competitor comparison, so the same terms can be read against rival domains.

items.name: Location
items.body: Location is part of the measurement, not a filter applied afterwards. The same keyword in two cities can return different results, and each is recorded with its own history.

items.name: Device
items.body: Desktop and mobile are checked and stored separately. Divergence between the two is one of the earliest signals of a mobile-specific problem.

monitoring.intro: A rank tracker is only useful if the measurement is repeated. Three things in SeeO exist specifically to make the repeated measurement readable.

items.name: Daily automatic refresh
items.body: A scheduled job refreshes tracked keywords once a day. You do not need to remember to run it, and you do not need to keep a spreadsheet alongside it.

items.name: Ranking history
items.body: Every refresh writes a dated record, so the full series behind each keyword stays available. History is read from the database and costs no provider calls.

items.name: Movement alerts
items.body: After each refresh SeeO compares the new position with the previous one. Significant movements — including a keyword dropping out of the top 100 entirely — produce an in-app alert with the old and new position.

items.name: Trend direction
items.body: Instead of comparing only two points, SeeO summarises recent direction from a window of past records. When there is not yet enough history to say anything reliable, it returns no direction rather than guessing.

reading.intro: Most ranking disappointment comes from reading a single number as if it were a verdict. These are the checks that make a rank report useful.

items.name: Compare like with like
items.body: Only compare records that share keyword, location, and device. A drop that appears when you switch device is a device signal, not a ranking collapse.

items.name: Treat small daily movement as noise
items.body: A one-position change between two days usually reflects normal SERP churn. Multi-day direction is the part worth acting on.

items.name: Separate lost from never ranked
items.body: A keyword that had a position and no longer does is a different situation from one that was never recorded in the top 100. SeeO labels these differently so you do not chase the wrong problem.

items.name: Read device divergence early
items.body: When desktop holds and mobile falls, the cause is usually page experience on mobile rather than the keyword or the content.

items.name: Connect movement to what you shipped
items.body: A ranking change is an observation, not an explanation. Pair it with a technical audit or a backlink check before concluding what caused it.

workflow.intro: Rank tracking works best as the measurement step in a loop, not as a standalone habit.

steps.title: Build the keyword set
steps.body: Start from keyword research rather than from whatever you happen to be optimising. A stable set is easier to read than one that changes every week.

steps.title: Fix the measurement conditions
steps.body: Choose location and device deliberately and then leave them alone. Changing conditions mid-campaign makes the history unreadable.

steps.title: Capture a baseline
steps.body: Record where things stand before you change anything. Without a baseline you cannot tell improvement from noise.

steps.title: Let the daily refresh accumulate
steps.body: A trend needs several data points. Give the schedule time before drawing conclusions.

steps.title: Investigate real movement
steps.body: When a keyword drops, check technical health and link changes before rewriting content. The cause is often not on the page.

steps.title: Report from the same record
steps.body: Export rank reports from the stored history so everyone reads the same numbers.

backlinks.whatItDoes: Backlink analysis is the process of examining the links pointing to a domain: how many there are, where they come from, which anchors they use, and whether the overall pattern looks natural. SeeO pulls a snapshot of that link profile and stores it, so you can work from the same data later instead of re-querying from scratch. Each query returns a summary — total backlinks, referring domains, Domain Rank, and dofollow ratio — plus individual link records with the source page, anchor text, target page, and first-seen date. Referring domain and anchor text distributions are computed from the stored link list, which is what turns a raw link dump into something you can actually read. SeeO is built for ongoing SEO work rather than for a single instant lookup. Results are cached for seven days per domain, so a profile you pulled this week stays available for comparison next week. The point is to see how a link profile changes after a campaign, not to grab one number and leave. You can run it on your own domain or on a competitor's. Comparing two profiles on the same metrics is usually the fastest way to turn a competitor's link list into a realistic target list.

sections.reading: How to read a link profile

metrics.intro: These are the fields SeeO returns. Knowing which of them answers which question is most of the skill in link profile analysis.

summary.name: Total backlinks
summary.body: The number of links found pointing at the domain in the provider's index. Useful as a scale indicator, weak as a quality indicator on its own.

summary.name: Referring domains
summary.body: How many distinct domains those links come from. Usually the more informative of the two counts.

summary.name: Domain Rank
summary.body: A strength score for the domain supplied by the data provider. Compare it between domains rather than reading it as an absolute value.

summary.name: Dofollow ratio
summary.body: The share of links that pass link equity. A profile with many links and a low dofollow ratio is not as strong as the raw count suggests.

linkLevel.name: Source page
linkLevel.body: The page carrying the link. This is what you open when you want to judge whether a link is editorially placed or dumped.

linkLevel.name: Anchor text
linkLevel.body: The clickable text. Anchor distribution is where over-optimisation shows up first.

linkLevel.name: Target page
linkLevel.body: Which of your pages the link points to. A profile concentrated on one URL looks different from one spread across a site.

linkLevel.name: Dofollow flag
linkLevel.body: Whether the link passes equity, recorded per link so the ratio can be recomputed for any subset.

linkLevel.name: First-seen date
linkLevel.body: When the provider first observed the link. Useful for correlating profile growth with a campaign period.

reading.intro: A link profile is a pattern, not a score. These are the checks that turn the stored link list into a judgement.

items.name: Read referring domains before total backlinks
items.body: A thousand links from ten domains is a very different profile from a thousand links from nine hundred. Domain count resists the inflation that raw link count is prone to.

items.name: Put the dofollow ratio in context
items.body: Some nofollow-heavy profiles are completely normal — directories, forums, and social platforms are nofollow by default. Compare against a similar site before treating a low ratio as a problem.

items.name: Look for anchor concentration
items.body: If one exact-match commercial phrase accounts for most anchors, that is the risk signal worth investigating, regardless of how good the totals look.

items.name: Use first-seen dates as timing evidence
items.body: Clusters of new links around a date usually mean a campaign, a mention, or a problem. The date tells you where to look.

items.name: Check target page spread
items.body: A profile where every link points at the homepage is structurally different from one spread across content. Neither is automatically wrong, but they support different strategies.

items.name: Remember the index is not the web
items.body: Every backlink provider crawls its own index. Counts differ between tools, and very new or very small sites are often under-represented.

workflow.intro: Backlink analysis pays off when it is attached to a decision rather than run out of curiosity.

steps.title: Baseline your own profile
steps.body: Capture your current link profile before starting anything. Without a baseline you cannot tell growth from noise.

steps.title: Pull the profiles you are competing against
steps.body: Query the domains that already rank for your target keywords. Competitor research works better on real rivals than on whoever is largest.

steps.title: Turn the difference into a target list
steps.body: Domains that link to several competitors but not to you are the realistic shortlist.

steps.title: Work the list, then re-query
steps.body: Because snapshots are cached for seven days, a re-query after a campaign shows net movement rather than a fresh random sample.

steps.title: Interpret alongside rankings
steps.body: Link profile change and ranking movement are two views of the same period. Read them together before attributing a cause.

intro: SeeO is an SEO analytics platform that helps site owners and SEO practitioners make search optimization decisions based on real data.

meta.title: How to Do a Technical SEO Audit: Step-by-Step Guide | SeeO
meta.description: A step-by-step technical SEO audit guide: crawl the site, check indexability, on-page basics, speed, mobile, security, structured data, then prioritize fixes.

guideTechnicalSeoAudit.title: How to Do a Technical SEO Audit (Step-by-Step)
guideTechnicalSeoAudit.subtitle: A practical framework for auditing a website's technical health — what to check, in what order, and how to prioritize fixes that actually move rankings
guideTechnicalSeoAudit.intro: A technical SEO audit reviews the foundation a site is built on: can search engines crawl and index it, is the on-page markup correct, does it load fast, and is it secure and mobile-friendly? This guide walks through a repeatable audit process you can run yourself, whether you use SeeO's audit tool or another crawler. Each step lists what to look for and why it matters, so you can turn a long to-do list into a prioritized plan.

steps.title: Crawl the site and inventory pages
steps.body: Start with a full crawl from your sitemap (or a crawler) so you have every indexable URL. Note the total page count and any crawl errors. A crawl is the baseline — without it you are guessing.

steps.title: Check indexability
steps.body: Review robots.txt, the XML sitemap, canonical tags, and noindex rules. Look for pages blocked from indexing, canonicals pointing to the wrong URL, and redirect chains that waste crawl budget.

steps.title: On-page basics
steps.body: For each important page, check the title tag, meta description, H1 hierarchy, and image alt text. These are the fundamentals search engines use to understand and rank a page.

steps.title: Site architecture and internal links
steps.body: Map how pages link to each other. Fix orphaned pages (no internal links), tighten deep click paths, and make sure important pages are reachable within a few clicks from the homepage.

steps.title: Page speed and Core Web Vitals
steps.body: Measure LCP, INP, and CLS. Slow pages hurt both rankings and users; prioritize templates and pages with the most traffic.

steps.title: Mobile-friendliness
steps.body: Confirm the site renders correctly on mobile, uses a responsive layout, and passes mobile usability checks. Most indexing is mobile-first, so this is not optional.

steps.title: HTTPS and security
steps.body: Verify the SSL certificate is valid and every page redirects to HTTPS. Mixed content and expired certificates are easy, high-impact fixes.

steps.title: Structured data
steps.body: Validate schema markup (Organization, Product, FAQ, BreadcrumbList, and others). Correct structured data can unlock rich results and clearer indexing.

steps.title: Backlinks and off-page signals
steps.body: Review the link profile: total backlinks, referring domains, and anchor text distribution. A sudden drop in referring domains often explains a rankings drop.

steps.title: Prioritize and track fixes
steps.body: Score issues by impact and sort them into a fix list. Re-audit after changes so you can prove the health score and rankings improved.

faqs.q: How often should I run a technical SEO audit?
faqs.a: At least once per quarter, and immediately after any redesign, migration, or platform change. Continuous monitoring catches regressions between full audits.

faqs.q: Do I need a paid tool to audit a site?
faqs.a: You can start with free crawlers and Search Console, but a tool like SeeO's audit automates the 20+ checks and keeps history so you can compare runs. The method in this guide works with any crawler.

faqs.q: What is the most important audit metric?
faqs.a: There is no single number, but indexability issues (pages that should be indexed but aren't) and Core Web Vitals tend to have the widest impact. Start there before cosmetic fixes.

faqs.q: How do I know if my fixes worked?
faqs.a: Re-run the audit and compare the health score and issue count against the previous run. Pair it with rank tracking so you can connect a fix to a ranking change.

meta.title: How to Track Keyword Rankings - SEO Position Tracking Guide | SeeO
meta.description: A practical guide to tracking keyword rankings: fix your measurement conditions, build a stable keyword set, and read ranking movement without fooling yourself.

guideKeywordRankings.title: How to Track Keyword Rankings
guideKeywordRankings.subtitle: A practical guide to keyword rank tracking and SEO position monitoring — what to measure, how often, and how to read the result without fooling yourself
guideKeywordRankings.intro: Almost everyone who starts doing SEO checks their rankings. Far fewer people set that check up so the numbers mean anything three months later. This guide covers the whole job: deciding what to track, fixing the conditions so the data stays comparable, choosing a cadence, and reading movement in a way that survives contact with reality. None of it requires a specific tool, but everything here assumes you are recording results rather than looking them up once.

steps.title: Decide what question the tracking answers
steps.body: Before adding a keyword, name the decision the data will inform. "Is our product page gaining ground on the main commercial term?" is a question. "Are we ranking well?" is not — it produces a dashboard nobody acts on. Write the question down; it determines which keywords belong in the set and which do not.
steps.why: A keyword set built from a real question stays stable. Sets built from curiosity get changed constantly, and every change resets the history you are trying to read.

steps.title: Fix the measurement conditions
steps.body: Choose the search engine, the location, and the device, then leave them alone. Record them somewhere. If you later need a second market or a second device, add it as a separate series rather than editing the existing one.
steps.why: Google does not return identical results for the same words in different places or on different devices. If conditions drift mid-campaign, the trend line measures your own inconsistency instead of your SEO.

steps.title: Choose a keyword set you can live with
steps.body: Mix a small number of commercially important head terms with a longer tail of specific terms you can realistically win. Group them by intent or by page so a movement points at something. Resist the urge to add every keyword you have ever researched.
steps.why: Large, ungrouped sets produce noise. A movement across one group is a signal; a movement across four hundred unrelated terms is weather.

steps.title: Capture a baseline before changing anything
steps.body: Record positions first, then start the work. If you change the page and only then begin tracking, you will never know whether the change helped or whether you were already moving.
steps.why: Without a baseline there is no before-and-after, only after. Most attribution arguments in SEO come from this single omission.

steps.title: Pick a cadence and keep it
steps.body: For most sites daily is right, weekly is acceptable, and ad hoc is useless. What matters more than frequency is consistency: the same interval, the same conditions, indefinitely.
steps.why: Trends are comparisons between measurements taken under the same rules. Irregular sampling makes the series unreadable regardless of how often you looked.

steps.title: Read ranges, not single points
steps.body: Treat a one- or two-position change between consecutive days as normal churn. Look for direction over several measurements. When a tool summarises trend for you, check how much history it requires before it will commit to a direction.
steps.why: SERP results move for reasons that have nothing to do with your site. Reacting to single-day movement produces constant, pointless work.

steps.title: Separate device and location signals
steps.body: When desktop holds position and mobile drops, suspect page experience on mobile rather than the content or the keyword. When one city drops and another holds, suspect local competition or localised results rather than a site-wide problem.
steps.why: These two splits localise the cause faster than any amount of staring at an aggregate number.

steps.title: Distinguish "lost" from "never ranked"
steps.body: A keyword that had a position and no longer appears is an event worth investigating. A keyword that was never recorded in the tracked range is a different situation entirely — usually a targeting or expectation problem rather than a regression.
steps.why: Conflating the two sends teams chasing losses that never existed and missing the drops that did.

steps.title: Investigate before you rewrite
steps.body: When a genuine drop appears, check technical health and link changes before touching the content. A lost internal link, a noindex that shipped by accident, or an expired redirect are all far more common causes than a sudden loss of topical relevance.
steps.why: Rewriting a page that dropped for technical reasons wastes the rewrite and leaves the real cause in place.

steps.title: Keep the record for reporting
steps.body: Export from the stored history rather than from screenshots. Report the question from step one alongside the numbers, so the reader knows what the movement means.
steps.why: Reporting that answers the original question gets acted on. Reporting that only shows positions gets skimmed.

caveats.title: What rank tracking cannot tell you
caveats.intro: Rank tracking is measurement, not diagnosis. Being clear about its limits prevents most of the wasted work that follows a rank report.
items: A position is an observation at one moment under one set of conditions; it is not a verdict on content quality.
Personalisation and SERP features mean two people can see different results for the same query on the same day.
Movement tells you something changed, never what changed. Attribution requires a second data source.
Ranking improvements and traffic improvements are related but not proportional — a rise from page two to the bottom of page one often moves very little traffic.
Tracking depth is finite. A position beyond the tracked range is recorded as unranked, which is not the same as invisible.

faqs.q: How often should I check keyword rankings?
faqs.a: Daily is the practical default if you are actively changing things, weekly if you are maintaining. The important part is consistency rather than frequency — irregular checks produce an unreadable series.

faqs.q: Should I track rankings on desktop, mobile, or both?
faqs.a: Both, if you can. Google indexes primarily from the mobile view, and desktop and mobile results genuinely differ. If you track only one, track the device your audience actually uses.

faqs.q: Why do my rankings look different from what I see in a browser?
faqs.a: Because results vary by location, device, language, and personalisation, and because SERP features occupy space above the first organic result. A tracked position is a controlled measurement, not a screenshot of your browser.

faqs.q: How many keywords should I track?
faqs.a: Enough to answer your question and no more. For most sites that means a handful of commercially important terms plus a few dozen specific ones, grouped by intent or by the page they target.

faqs.q: My rankings dropped. What should I do first?
faqs.a: Confirm the drop is real by checking the full series and the conditions, then look for technical and link changes before editing content. Genuine regressions usually have a mechanical cause.

guideBacklinkAnalysis.title: How to Analyze Backlinks
guideBacklinkAnalysis.subtitle: A practical guide to backlink analysis and link profile analysis — which numbers matter, how to read anchor and domain patterns, and where the data misleads
guideBacklinkAnalysis.intro: Backlink data is easy to obtain and easy to misread. A tool will hand you a total, and the total is almost always the least useful number in the report. This guide walks through the job in the order that actually works: start from a question, take a baseline, read the composition rather than the count, compare against the domains you are competing with, and only then decide what to do. It also covers where backlink data genuinely misleads, which is most of the value.

steps.title: Start with the question, not the tool
steps.body: Decide what you are investigating before you query anything. "Which domains link to three of our competitors but not to us?" is actionable. "How strong is our backlink profile?" produces a number and no decision.
steps.why: The question determines which metrics matter. Chasing a total when the real question is about target domains wastes the query and the afternoon.

steps.title: Take a baseline of your own profile
steps.body: Query your own domain first and store the result. Note the total backlinks, referring domains, dofollow ratio, and the shape of the anchor distribution. Do this before you change anything.
steps.why: Every later judgement is a comparison. Without a baseline you are reading numbers in a vacuum and will over-interpret ordinary fluctuation.

steps.title: Read referring domains before total backlinks
steps.body: Look at how many distinct domains the links come from, not how many links exist. Ten thousand links from twenty domains is a much weaker profile than a thousand links from eight hundred.
steps.why: Link counts inflate naturally — one site template can generate thousands of links. Domain counts resist that inflation and correlate better with actual link equity.

steps.title: Put the dofollow ratio in context
steps.body: Check what share of links pass equity, then compare it against a similar site rather than against an ideal. Directories, forums, and social platforms are frequently nofollow by default.
steps.why: A low dofollow ratio is often just a normal profile shape. Without a comparison you will treat ordinary composition as a defect.

steps.title: Read the anchor text distribution
steps.body: Look at how anchors are spread across branded, naked URL, generic, and exact-match commercial phrases. Concentration in one commercial phrase is the signal that matters, not the presence of exact-match anchors.
steps.why: Anchor concentration is where over-optimisation becomes visible. Totals and ratios can look healthy right up until the anchor distribution shows the problem.

steps.title: Open the source pages
steps.body: Do not judge a link from the domain name. Open a sample of source pages and ask whether the link is editorially placed, sits in relevant content, and would exist if the site owner had not been asked.
steps.why: Two links from the same domain can differ enormously in value. Only the source page tells you which kind you have.

steps.title: Check target page spread
steps.body: See which of your URLs the links point at. A profile concentrated on the homepage supports different strategies from one spread across content pages.
steps.why: Internal link equity follows the target page. If you are trying to rank a specific page, links to the homepage do much less for it than the totals suggest.

steps.title: Compare against the domains that actually outrank you
steps.body: Query the sites ranking above you for your target keywords, not the largest sites in your industry. Look for domains appearing in several competitor profiles but not in yours.
steps.why: Those shared-but-missing domains are the realistic target list. Links held by a much larger competitor are often not winnable and make a poor plan.

steps.title: Watch change over time, not just snapshot state
steps.body: Re-query on a fixed interval and compare like with like. Use first-seen dates to correlate new links with campaign periods.
steps.why: A snapshot tells you where you are; a series tells you whether your work is landing. Timing evidence turns a vague impression into a causal claim you can test.

steps.title: Write down what you concluded
steps.body: Record the question, the comparison, and the decision. Note what you expect to happen next and when you will check.
steps.why: Backlink work compounds slowly. Without a written conclusion, the next review starts from zero and repeats the same analysis.

caveats.title: Where backlink data misleads
caveats.intro: Backlink data comes from a provider's own crawl, and every number in it carries assumptions. These are the ones that cause the most bad decisions.
items: No provider sees the whole web. Counts differ between tools, and the difference is normal rather than a sign that one of them is wrong.
Very new and very small sites are systematically under-represented. A thin profile may mean thin coverage as much as thin links.
Links appear and disappear from an index with a delay, so recent work is usually invisible in the data for a while.
A large share of stored links for a big domain may be a sample rather than a complete inventory. Composition is still readable; totals are not.
A high total says nothing about relevance. A small number of topically close links routinely outperforms a large number of unrelated ones.

faqs.q: What is link profile analysis?
faqs.a: It is the examination of all links pointing to a domain — where they come from, which anchors they use, which pages they target, and whether the overall pattern looks naturally earned. The output is a judgement about the profile, not a single score.

faqs.q: Which matters more, total backlinks or referring domains?
faqs.a: Referring domains, almost always. Distinct domains resist the inflation that raw link counts are prone to, and they correlate better with real link equity.

faqs.q: Why do different tools report different backlink numbers?
faqs.a: Each provider maintains its own index with its own crawl, discovery rules, and update cadence. Differences are expected; consistency within one tool over time is what makes the data usable.

faqs.q: How often should I analyze my backlinks?
faqs.a: Monthly suits most sites, and around a campaign it is worth checking before and after. The important thing is comparing snapshots taken under the same conditions.

faqs.q: Can backlink analysis tell me why my rankings dropped?
faqs.a: On its own, no. It can show that a link disappeared or that a competitor gained ground, which is evidence to combine with ranking and technical data — not a complete explanation.

metrics.title: What the numbers mean
metrics.intro: Four numbers, four different questions. They disagree with each other often, and that disagreement is the useful part.

items.name: Total backlinks
items.body: Every link the provider found pointing at the domain. It is a raw count: 10,000 links from a single blog is not the same as 10,000 links from 10,000 different sites.

items.name: Referring domains
items.body: How many distinct sites link to the domain. This is usually the number that tracks with authority, which is why it sits next to the raw total rather than behind it.

items.name: Domain Rank
items.body: The provider's 0-100 authority score for the domain as a whole. Read it against the sites you compete with, never against an absolute target.

items.name: Dofollow share
items.body: The percentage of links that pass ranking signals. A profile that is mostly nofollow is common and is not automatically a problem — what matters is which pages carry the dofollow links.

reading.title: How to read a backlink profile
reading.intro: A backlink count on its own does not tell you much. These four habits turn the preview into an actual judgment.

items.name: Start with referring domains
items.body: One strong site linking to you moves more than a thousand links from a directory nobody reads. When the two numbers diverge sharply, the smaller one is usually the honest one.

items.name: Compare against whoever outranks you
items.body: Run the same check on the pages above yours. A gap in referring domains explains a ranking gap far more often than a gap in total links does.

items.name: Read source ranks, not totals
items.body: Look at the ranks of the linking pages in the sample below. Five links from respected sites tell a different story from five links from freshly registered domains.

items.name: Re-check later instead of judging once
items.body: Link profiles change slowly. One snapshot is a photograph; the same snapshot taken a month apart is evidence of whether your outreach is working.

faqs.q: Where does the data come from?

faqs.q: How current is the data?
faqs.a: Each domain is fetched on demand and then cached for seven days. The result shows the timestamp of the snapshot and whether you are looking at a cached copy or a freshly fetched one.

faqs.q: Why do I only see five links?

faqs.q: Why do these numbers differ from another backlink tool?
faqs.a: Every backlink index is built by crawling, and each vendor crawls a different slice of the web. Different indexes produce different totals, so compare a tool against itself over time rather than expecting two vendors to agree.

faqs.q: Do I need an account to check a domain?

faqs.q: Is there a limit on how many domains I can check?

faqs.q: Can I check a competitor's backlinks?
